transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess what brings me in is… since I stopped working, I just can’t seem to slow down. I’m up and moving all day, going from one little job to the next, like there’s still a crew waiting on me or something.

I’ll start one thing, then notice something else that needs doing, and before I know it I’ve been on my feet all day. Used to be, that kind of pace made sense at work, you know? There was always somebody needing something, always another task. Now it’s just me at home, but my body still acts like I’ve got to keep moving.
When you’re in this go-go mode, do you find that you need less sleep than usual?

I’m not really sure. I mean, I’m up and moving a lot, but I haven’t paid close attention to whether I’m actually sleeping less. Some nights I’m in bed and my mind’s kind of… well, I start thinking about the garage or the yard, and then I remember this old job I had where we’d be up before dawn—but that’s not exactly what you’re asking, is it?

So, no, I don’t think I’ve noticed needing less sleep, not clearly.
When you get into this go-go mode, do you also feel unusually upbeat or excited?

Unusually upbeat… I don’t know that I’d say that. I mean, sometimes I feel good if I’m getting things done, like if the shed finally looks halfway decent, that’s satisfying. But excited, like really wound up happy? I’m not sure.

It’s more like I just keep moving. My wife used to say I’d pace around even when there wasn’t much to do, and I’d tell her, well, there’s always something—though half the time I’d end up reorganizing a drawer instead of finishing what I started. But as far as feeling especially upbeat, I haven’t really noticed that.
When you keep busy like this, do you feel driven to do it because unwanted thoughts or a strong sense that you have to?

I’m not sure I’d call it unwanted thoughts exactly. I mean, sometimes I’ll see something sitting out and it kind of nags at me, like, “Well, I should put that away,” and then that turns into three other things.

But a strong sense that I have to… I don’t know. It’s not like a voice in my head or some terrible thought I’m trying to get rid of. It’s more that I notice one thing, then another, and I’m already up anyway. Like yesterday I went to take out the trash and ended up checking the side gate, then looking at the hose, and then I remembered this time years ago when we had a leak behind the garage—sorry, I’m wandering.

So… I guess I haven’t really noticed it being because of unwanted thoughts. It’s more just, I get going and don’t stop.
When you were a child, were you already the kind of person who got distracted easily and jumped from one task to another?

Yeah, I think so. Even in grade school, I remember teachers saying I was bright, but kind of scattered. I’d lose pencils all the time—my mother used to get annoyed because she’d buy those big packs, and somehow they’d just disappear.

And I’d call out answers, too, before I was supposed to. Then I’d need reminders to finish my work before recess, because I’d start one thing and then be looking out the window or messing with something in my desk. So… yes, I guess that was already there pretty early.
Do you often find yourself worrying a lot about everyday things, even when there isn’t a clear reason to?

Worrying a lot… I don’t know. I mean, I worry about the normal stuff, I guess—bills, whether I remembered to lock the door, if the car’s making some noise it shouldn’t. But I wouldn’t say I’m sitting around worrying all day for no reason.

Sometimes something will get in my head and I’ll circle back to it, like if I need to call someone and then I forget, then remember it while I’m doing something else. Actually, that happened with the insurance papers once—well, not important.

So… I’m not sure. I haven’t really thought of myself as a big worrier, no.
When you keep moving like this, do you feel on guard, like you need to stay alert for something bad to happen?

On guard… hmm. I don’t think so, not really. I mean, if I hear a noise outside at night I’ll notice it, but I think most people would. It’s not like I’m moving around because I think something bad is about to happen.

It’s more like I just get up to do one thing, and then—well, like the other day I went to check if the back door was shut, and then I saw the mail on the table, and then I remembered I hadn’t watered the plant by the window. That plant’s been half-dead for years anyway, my wife used to say I either drowned it or forgot it completely.

But no, I don’t think I feel alert for danger exactly. I haven’t really noticed that.
Did this getting-up-and-going all day become noticeably worse after you stopped working?

Yeah, I’d say that’s when it really got noticeable. When I was working, I was always moving anyway, so it just seemed normal—like there was always another job to get to, somebody needing something, that sort of thing.

But since I stopped working, I still can’t really slow down. I’m up and down all day, going from one little thing to the next, like there’s still a crew waiting on me or I’m supposed to be somewhere. I’ll start to sit, then think of something in the garage, then the trash, then some little thing in the kitchen… it just keeps going.
Did anything traumatic happen around the time you stopped working?

Traumatic? No, I don’t think so. I mean, stopping work was strange, sure—after doing it for so many years, suddenly your day doesn’t have the same shape to it.

But nothing like an accident or… I don’t know, something terrible happening right then. It was more just a change. I remember cleaning out my locker and finding old receipts and a pair of gloves I thought I’d lost, and then I brought all that junk home and it sat by the garage door for weeks.

So, no, not that I can think of.
Have being easily distracted and jumping from one task to another caused problems for you in daily life?

Yeah… it has, I suppose. I don’t like saying that, but yes.

My wife ended up sort of taking over the calendar, because I’d say I was going to be somewhere and then I’d get caught up doing something else, or I’d start one thing and forget the other thing completely. She checks behind me more than I’d like to admit.

And I’ve had to apologize to the community center and the garden group a few times, too. I meant to bring something, or show up for something, and then… well, I didn’t follow through. The garden group had this whole thing with mulch one Saturday—funny how much people can argue about mulch—but anyway, yes, I let people down more than once.
Even when you try to relax, do you feel restless or unable to stay seated for very long?

Yes, I do. Even if I’m trying to relax, like sitting through a quiet meeting or one of those church talks, I start feeling like I need to move around.

I’ll shift in the seat, tap my foot, stretch my legs out, then pull them back in… that sort of thing. Sometimes I’m thinking, “Just sit still, you’re a grown man,” but then my back feels tight or my knee starts bouncing. Church pews don’t help either—never built for comfort, if you ask me.

But yes, even when I know I’m supposed to stay put, I get that feeling like I ought to get up and stretch or move around.
When you get like this, do other people tell you that you’re talking more than usual?

I’m not sure, honestly. My wife might say something if I get going, but I don’t know if that’s “more than usual” or just me telling a story badly.

I mean, some people tell stories straight from A to B, and I’ll remember something about a neighbor’s dog or what happened at the hardware store, and then I’ve taken the scenic route. But as far as people saying, “You’re talking too much today,” no… I don’t really recall that being a regular thing.
Have there been times when you felt unusually confident, like you could do things better than other people or take on more than was realistic?

Not really, no… I mean, I’ve had moments where I thought, “Oh, I can handle that,” and then it turned out to be more of a project than I expected. Like trying to fix something around the house and ending up with parts laid out everywhere—my wife still reminds me about a cabinet hinge I “definitely knew how to fix.”

But unusually confident, like I’m better than other people or can take on the world? No, I don’t think so. If anything, I usually second-guess myself more than that.
Do you often lose or misplace الأشياء you need, like keys, papers, or tools?

Oh yes, all the time. I spend a ridiculous amount of time hunting for my glasses, my keys, the tape measure… and I’ve got this little notebook I use for story ideas, and that disappears on me too.

The funny thing is, half the time I just had the thing in my hand a few minutes before. I’ll walk into another room, set it down somewhere “safe,” and then I’m checking the kitchen counter, the chair, the garage… My wife will say, “Did you look where you were just standing?” and darn if she isn’t usually right.
Do you repeatedly check things like locks, doors, or appliances even after you know you already checked them?

I don’t think so… not repeatedly, anyway. I mean, I’ll check the front door at night, sure, but I think most people do that. Sometimes I’ll stand there a second and wonder if I turned the porch light off, and then I’ll remember we started leaving it on because of that raccoon that kept getting into the trash—well, I guess that’s not really what you asked.

No, I don’t believe I’m going back over and over to check locks or the stove or things like that after I already know I checked them.
